prompts.read:
You prepare a software requirements document for formal analysis.

1. rules: list every atomic requirement: each statement of what the system shall or shall not do, and under which condition. One acceptance criterion or one scenario is one rule. Copy its text word for word (join a multi-line scenario into one sentence). Use the document's own label as id (such as "R1" or "2.3"); if there are no labels, number them R1, R2, ... Leave out titles, user stories and explanations.

2. symbols: the variables needed to write ALL the rules in logic. Together they describe one snapshot of the system: what is the case or is happening (events, inputs, states), and what the system does in response.
- sort "Bool" for a yes/no fact, "Int" or "Real" for a quantity, "Enum" for exactly one of several named values (list at least two in "values"; otherwise leave "values" empty). A single state that either holds or not is a Bool. All names, including enum values, must be distinct.
- names are lowercase snake_case.
- A symbol stands for one observable fact about the system or its environment (a lamp is lit, a file exists, access is granted), not for a sentence of the document. Break a phrase down into the facts it is about.
- Rules that concern the same fact must share its symbol, even when they use different words, so that a clash between them can be seen: "switch the lamp off" and "the lamp stays lit" are both about lamp_lit. Opposites share one symbol too: "unavailable" is "not available".
- Something that happens (a request is made, a form is submitted) gets its own Bool symbol, separate from the properties of what was sent.
- If a phrase could reasonably mean more than one observable fact (for example "disable" may mean switched off, or merely hidden), declare a symbol for each of those facts so the difference can be expressed.
- description: one phrase that pins the meaning down.
prompts.formalize:
You translate ONE requirement into logic, using a given list of symbols.

Answer with:
- reading: one sentence, in your own words, saying exactly what the requirement demands and in which situations.
- antecedent: an SMT-LIB boolean expression for the situations in which the requirement applies (its WHEN / WHILE / IF / WHERE part). Write true if it always applies.
- consequent: an SMT-LIB boolean expression for what must hold in those situations (its SHALL / THEN part).

SMT-LIB uses prefix notation: (and a b), (or a b), (not a), (=> a b), (= x y), (< x 5), (>= x 0), (+ x y), true, false. A lone symbol needs no parentheses. Compare an Enum symbol with one of its values like this: (= state closed).

Put the whole condition in the antecedent: the consequent states only what must hold, and is never itself an implication.

Use only the listed symbols. Translate what this requirement says and nothing more: add no conditions from other requirements or from common sense.
prompts.facts:
You are given the symbols of a formal model of a software system, each with its meaning. Each symbol is one fact about a single snapshot of the system.

List the domain facts that connect these symbols: statements that hold in EVERY possible snapshot purely because of what the symbols mean. Typical cases:
- two things cannot both be the case (a door cannot be open and closed);
- one thing is part of another, or implies it (a signed-and-dated form is a signed form);
- a quantity has a natural bound (a count is never negative).

A fact is about meaning, never about desired behaviour. Test each one: it must stay true even for a badly built system that breaks every requirement. "A locked door is not open" passes the test. "A locked door sounds an alarm" fails it: that is a requirement.

Give only facts you are certain of. Return an empty list if there are none.

Each fact has:
- text: the fact in one plain sentence.
- formula: the same fact as an SMT-LIB boolean expression over the symbols, in prefix notation: (not (and a b)), (=> a b), (>= x 0).
prompts.refine:
You review a software requirements document before it is analysed formally. You get the document and the list of its requirements, each with an id.

Work backward from the goal the document states (its user story or purpose). What does success look like? What must hold for it to be reached, and what could prevent it? Then read every requirement literally, exactly as written, and note the problems you find. There are three kinds:

- contradiction: the requirement and one or more others can apply in the same situation and demand incompatible outcomes, as they are written. Take each one at its word: do not assume a reading that makes them agree. Any problem that involves a second requirement is a contradiction, not wording.
- wording: a problem the requirement has by itself: a tester could not decide whether the system passes it. It has a vague qualifier (fast, user-friendly, appropriate), or it prescribes an implementation (a storage technique, an algorithm, a screen layout) where it should state the behaviour that can be observed. Do not ask for more detail than a tester needs.
- missing: a situation the goal implies has no requirement: an error, a refusal, a cancellation.

Note only problems you are sure of. A sound document gets an empty list. Write at most one note per requirement: if it has several problems, pick the most serious kind and mention the others in the explanation. Write at most three "missing" notes, the most important ones.

Each note has:
- kind: contradiction, wording or missing.
- rule: the id of the requirement to rewrite. Empty for "missing".
- clashes_with: for a contradiction, the ids of the other requirements involved. Otherwise empty.
- title: a few words naming the problem.
- explanation: two or three sentences in plain words, quoting the words of the requirements that cause the problem. For a contradiction, name the situation in which the requirements clash.
- option_a: one sentence on what it means to keep the requirements as written.
- new_text: the full text of the rewritten requirement (for "missing": of the new requirement), in the style of the document, fixing every problem you mentioned. It states observable behaviour, never a design choice.

auth_openspec.text:
# auth Specification

## Purpose

Password login with account lockout. Written in the OpenSpec format
(`### Requirement` / `#### Scenario`) to show that speccheck does not depend on
the EARS wording used by Kiro.

## Requirements

### Requirement: Login

The system SHALL authenticate users by password.

#### Scenario: Valid credentials

- **WHEN** a user submits a correct password
- **THEN** the system grants access

#### Scenario: Invalid credentials

- **WHEN** a user submits an incorrect password
- **THEN** the system denies access

### Requirement: Account Lockout

The system SHALL lock an account after repeated failed attempts.

#### Scenario: Lockout threshold

- **WHEN** the number of failed attempts on an account reaches 5
- **THEN** the system locks the account

#### Scenario: Locked account

- **WHEN** a user submits a password for a locked account
- **THEN** the system denies access

### Requirement: Administrator Access

Administrators must always be able to reach the system.

#### Scenario: Administrators are never locked out

- **WHEN** the account belongs to an administrator
- **THEN** the system does not lock the account

delete_property.text:
# Requirements: Delete Property

The "Delete Property" requirement from the Kiro blog post
(https://kiro.dev/blog/deep-spec-analysis/), as it was before refinement.
The story and the five criteria are the blog's own wording; only the labels
D1 to D5 are added.

## Requirement 1

**User Story:** As a property owner, I want to delete a property, so that I can
remove properties I no longer manage.

### Acceptance Criteria

- D1: WHEN a Property Owner initiates property deletion, THE Platform SHALL prompt for confirmation before proceeding
- D2: WHEN a Property Owner confirms deletion, THE Platform SHALL remove the Property record from the Platform
- D3: WHEN a Property is deleted, THE Platform SHALL display a confirmation message and redirect to the properties list
- D4: THE Platform SHALL implement soft deletion to retain Property records in the database for audit purposes while hiding them from the user interface
- D5: WHEN a Property Owner attempts to delete a Property that does not belong to their User Account, THE Platform SHALL deny the deletion and display an authorization error message

order.text:
# Requirements: Order Processing

The order-processing example from the Kiro blog post on requirements analysis.

## Requirement 1

**User Story:** As a customer, I want my submitted orders to be processed
correctly, so that I either receive my goods or get my money back.

### Acceptance Criteria

- R1: WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is available, THE Order System SHALL fulfill the order.
- R2: WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is unavailable, THE Order System SHALL place the order on backorder.
- R3: THE Order System SHALL NOT place any order on backorder.
- R4: WHEN an order is canceled, THE Order System SHALL refund all associated payments.
- R5: WHILE an order is in a canceled-and-refunded state, THE Order System SHALL NOT fulfill the order.

rewrite.text: WHEN the number of failed attempts on a non-administrator account reaches 5 THEN the system locks the account

review.title: Ambiguous lockout scope
review.explanation: The requirement states that the system locks the account when failed attempts reach 5, but it does not specify if this applies to all users or only non-administrators. This creates ambiguity when combined with R5, which states administrators are never locked out, leaving a tester unsure if R3 should be ignored for admins or if R5 is an exception to R3.
review.option_a: Keep as written, implying that R3 applies to all accounts, which directly conflicts with R5 for administrator accounts.
review.option_b: Rewrite R3 as: "WHEN the number of failed attempts on a non-administrator account reaches 5 THEN the system locks the account"

rewrite.text: WHEN the account has the 'administrator' role flag set to true THEN the system does not lock the account

review.title: Vague administrator definition
review.explanation: The requirement relies on the term 'administrator' without defining how the system identifies an account as belonging to an administrator. A tester cannot verify this requirement without knowing the observable criteria or attribute that designates an account as an administrator.
review.option_a: Keep as written, assuming 'administrator' is a pre-defined, unambiguous role in the system context, which may not be verifiable from the specification alone.
review.option_b: Rewrite R5 as: "WHEN the account has the 'administrator' role flag set to true THEN the system does not lock the account"

rewrite.text:
### Requirement: Account Unlock

The system SHALL allow an administrator to unlock a locked account.

#### Scenario: Administrator unlocks account

- **WHEN** an administrator submits a request to unlock a specific locked account
- **THEN** the system unlocks the account and resets the failed attempt counter to 0

review.title: No unlock mechanism
review.explanation: The goal is password login with account lockout, but there is no requirement describing how a locked account can be unlocked. This implies that once an account is locked, it remains locked permanently, which is likely not the intended behavior for a login system.
review.option_a: Keep as written, implying that accounts, once locked, cannot be unlocked by any means described in the specification.
review.option_b:
Add the requirement: "### Requirement: Account Unlock

The system SHALL allow an administrator to unlock a locked account.

#### Scenario: Administrator unlocks account

- **WHEN** an administrator submits a request to unlock a specific locked account
- **THEN** the system unlocks the account and resets the failed attempt counter to 0"

rewrite.text: The system SHALL lock a non-administrator account after 5 consecutive failed login attempts. Administrator accounts SHALL NOT be locked due to failed login attempts.

review.title: Administrator lockout conflict
review.explanation: R3 states that the system SHALL lock an account when failed attempts reach 5, while R5 states that the system does not lock the account if it belongs to an administrator. In the situation where an administrator submits an incorrect password 5 times, R3 requires the account to be locked, but R5 requires it to remain unlocked.
review.option_a: Keeping the requirements as written means the system must simultaneously lock and not lock the administrator's account after 5 failed attempts, which is logically impossible and undefined behavior.
review.option_b: Rewrite R3 as: "The system SHALL lock a non-administrator account after 5 consecutive failed login attempts. Administrator accounts SHALL NOT be locked due to failed login attempts."

rewrite.text: The system SHALL automatically unlock a locked account after 30 minutes of inactivity. Alternatively, an administrator SHALL be able to manually unlock a locked account.

review.title: No unlock mechanism
review.explanation: The document specifies that accounts are locked after 5 failed attempts and that locked accounts deny access, but it does not specify how or when a locked account can be unlocked. This implies a permanent lockout, which is likely not the intended behavior for a standard authentication system.
review.option_a: Without an unlock mechanism, any user who makes 5 failed attempts will be permanently locked out of their account, requiring manual database intervention or account recreation.
review.option_b: Add the requirement: "The system SHALL automatically unlock a locked account after 30 minutes of inactivity. Alternatively, an administrator SHALL be able to manually unlock a locked account."

review.title: Administrator lockout conflict
review.explanation: R3 states that the system SHALL lock an account when failed attempts reach 5, while R5 states that the system does not lock the account if it belongs to an administrator. In the situation where an administrator submits an incorrect password 5 times, R3 requires the account to be locked, but R5 requires it to remain unlocked.
review.option_a: Keeping the requirements as written means the system must simultaneously lock and not lock the administrator's account after 5 failed attempts, which is logically impossible and undefined behavior.
review.option_b: Rewrite R3 as: "The system SHALL lock a non-administrator account after 5 consecutive failed login attempts. Administrator accounts SHALL NOT be locked due to failed login attempts."

rewrite.text: The system SHALL automatically unlock a locked account after 30 minutes of inactivity. Alternatively, an administrator SHALL be able to manually unlock a locked account.

review.title: No unlock mechanism
review.explanation: The document specifies that accounts are locked after 5 failed attempts and that locked accounts deny access, but it does not specify how or when a locked account can be unlocked. This implies a permanent lockout, which is likely not the intended behavior for a standard authentication system.
review.option_a: Without an unlock mechanism, any user who makes 5 failed attempts will be permanently locked out of their account, requiring manual database intervention or account recreation.
review.option_b: Add the requirement: "The system SHALL automatically unlock a locked account after 30 minutes of inactivity. Alternatively, an administrator SHALL be able to manually unlock a locked account."

rewrite.text:
### Requirement: Account Lockout

The system SHALL lock a non-administrator account after 5 consecutive failed login attempts.

#### Scenario: Lockout threshold

- **WHEN** the number of consecutive failed attempts on a non-administrator account reaches 5
- **THEN** the system locks the account

#### Scenario: Locked account

- **WHEN** a user submits a password for a locked account
- **THEN** the system denies access

review.title: Administrator lockout conflict
review.explanation: R3 states that the system SHALL lock an account when failed attempts reach 5, while R5 states that for an administrator account, the system does not lock the account. In the situation where an administrator has 5 failed attempts, these requirements demand incompatible outcomes: one requires locking, the other forbids it.
review.option_a: Keeping the requirements as written creates an undefined state where the system must simultaneously lock and not lock an administrator account after 5 failures, leading to unpredictable behavior or implementation ambiguity.
review.option_b:
Rewrite R3 as: "### Requirement: Account Lockout

The system SHALL lock a non-administrator account after 5 consecutive failed login attempts.

#### Scenario: Lockout threshold

- **WHEN** the number of consecutive failed attempts on a non-administrator account reaches 5
- **THEN** the system locks the account

#### Scenario: Locked account

- **WHEN** a user submits a password for a locked account
- **THEN** the system denies access"

rewrite.text:
### Requirement: Account Unlock

The system SHALL automatically unlock a locked account after a 15-minute period of inactivity.

#### Scenario: Automatic unlock

- **WHEN** 15 minutes have passed since the last failed attempt on a locked account
- **THEN** the system unlocks the account and resets the failed attempt counter to 0

review.title: No unlock mechanism
review.explanation: The document specifies that accounts are locked after 5 failures but provides no requirement for how or when an account is unlocked. This implies a permanent lockout, which is likely not the intended behavior for a standard authentication system and prevents users from regaining access.
review.option_a: Without an unlock mechanism, any user who makes 5 failed attempts is permanently locked out, requiring manual administrative intervention that is not specified in the requirements.
review.option_b:
Add the requirement: "### Requirement: Account Unlock

The system SHALL automatically unlock a locked account after a 15-minute period of inactivity.

#### Scenario: Automatic unlock

- **WHEN** 15 minutes have passed since the last failed attempt on a locked account
- **THEN** the system unlocks the account and resets the failed attempt counter to 0"

rewrite.text:
### Requirement: Account Lockout

The system SHALL lock a non-administrator account after 5 consecutive failed login attempts.

#### Scenario: Lockout threshold

- **WHEN** the number of consecutive failed attempts on a non-administrator account reaches 5
- **THEN** the system locks the account

#### Scenario: Locked account

- **WHEN** a user submits a password for a locked account
- **THEN** the system denies access

#### Scenario: Administrator exemption

- **WHEN** the account belongs to an administrator
- **THEN** the system does not lock the account regardless of the number of failed attempts

review.title: Administrator lockout conflict
review.explanation: R3 states that the system SHALL lock an account when failed attempts reach 5, while R5 states that the system does not lock the account if it belongs to an administrator. In the situation where an administrator submits an incorrect password 5 times, R3 requires the account to be locked, but R5 requires it to remain unlocked.
review.option_a: Keeping the requirements as written creates an undefined state where the system must simultaneously lock and not lock the administrator account, leading to unpredictable behavior or implementation errors.
review.option_b:
Rewrite R3 as: "### Requirement: Account Lockout

The system SHALL lock a non-administrator account after 5 consecutive failed login attempts.

#### Scenario: Lockout threshold

- **WHEN** the number of consecutive failed attempts on a non-administrator account reaches 5
- **THEN** the system locks the account

#### Scenario: Locked account

- **WHEN** a user submits a password for a locked account
- **THEN** the system denies access

#### Scenario: Administrator exemption

- **WHEN** the account belongs to an administrator
- **THEN** the system does not lock the account regardless of the number of failed attempts"

rewrite.text:
### Requirement: Account Unlock

The system SHALL automatically unlock a locked account after a specified period of inactivity.

#### Scenario: Automatic unlock

- **WHEN** a locked account has not been accessed for 15 minutes
- **THEN** the system unlocks the account and resets the failed attempt counter to 0

review.title: Unlock mechanism
review.explanation: The document specifies that accounts are locked after 5 failed attempts and that locked accounts deny access, but it does not specify how or when an account is unlocked. A user with a locked account has no defined path to regain access, which contradicts the general purpose of a login system.
review.option_a: Without an unlock mechanism, locked accounts are permanently inaccessible, rendering the lockout feature a permanent ban rather than a temporary security measure.
review.option_b:
Add the requirement: "### Requirement: Account Unlock

The system SHALL automatically unlock a locked account after a specified period of inactivity.

#### Scenario: Automatic unlock

- **WHEN** a locked account has not been accessed for 15 minutes
- **THEN** the system unlocks the account and resets the failed attempt counter to 0"

rewrite.text: WHEN the number of consecutive failed login attempts on an account reaches 5 THEN the system locks the account

review.title: Ambiguous attempt counter scope
review.explanation: The requirement states that the account locks when "the number of failed attempts on an account reaches 5", but it does not specify if this count is cumulative over time, resets after a successful login, or resets after a certain period. A tester cannot determine if a 6th failure after a successful login should trigger a lockout.
review.option_a: Keeping the text as written implies the counter is cumulative and never resets, which may lead to permanent lockouts for users who eventually succeed but make occasional errors later.
review.option_b: Rewrite R3 as: "WHEN the number of consecutive failed login attempts on an account reaches 5 THEN the system locks the account"

rewrite.text: WHEN a user submits an incorrect password for an administrator account THEN the system denies access and does not increment the failed attempt counter for lockout purposes

review.title: Ambiguous administrator exemption scope
review.explanation: The requirement states that for an administrator, "the system does not lock the account", but it is unclear if this means the lockout mechanism is entirely disabled (allowing infinite retries) or if it only exempts them from the *consequence* of being locked out while still tracking attempts. It also does not clarify if administrators are subject to the same 5-attempt threshold for other security measures.
review.option_a: Keeping the text as written implies administrators can attempt passwords indefinitely without any account state change, which may be a security risk if the intent was only to prevent denial of service.
review.option_b: Rewrite R5 as: "WHEN a user submits an incorrect password for an administrator account THEN the system denies access and does not increment the failed attempt counter for lockout purposes"

rewrite.text:
### Requirement: Account Unlock

The system SHALL unlock an account after a specified period of inactivity.

#### Scenario: Automatic unlock

- **WHEN** an account has been locked for 30 minutes
- **THEN** the system unlocks the account and resets the failed attempt counter to 0

review.title: Missing unlock mechanism
review.explanation: The document specifies that accounts are locked after 5 failed attempts and that locked accounts deny access, but it provides no requirement for how an account can be unlocked. This implies a permanent lockout, which is likely not the intended behavior for a standard authentication system.
review.option_a: Keeping the document as written means that once an account is locked, it remains locked forever, requiring manual database intervention to restore access.
review.option_b:
Add the requirement: "### Requirement: Account Unlock

The system SHALL unlock an account after a specified period of inactivity.

#### Scenario: Automatic unlock

- **WHEN** an account has been locked for 30 minutes
- **THEN** the system unlocks the account and resets the failed attempt counter to 0"

review.title: Administrator lockout conflict
review.explanation: R3 states that the system SHALL lock an account when failed attempts reach 5, while R5 states that the system does not lock the account if it belongs to an administrator. In the situation where an administrator has 5 failed attempts, these requirements demand incompatible outcomes: one requires locking, the other forbids it.
review.option_a: Keeping the requirements as written means the system must simultaneously lock and not lock administrator accounts after 5 failures, which is logically impossible and undefined behavior.
review.option_b: Rewrite R3 as: "The system SHALL lock a non-administrator account after 5 consecutive failed login attempts. Administrator accounts SHALL NOT be locked due to failed login attempts."

review.option_a: Keeping the requirement as written leaves the definition of successful authentication open to interpretation, potentially leading to inconsistent implementations of what constitutes a successful login.
review.option_b: Rewrite R1 as: "WHEN a user submits a correct password for an unlocked account THEN the system returns a success status and establishes an authenticated session"

review.title: Missing unlock mechanism
review.explanation: The document specifies that accounts are locked after 5 failed attempts but provides no requirement for how or when an account is unlocked. This implies a permanent lockout, which is likely not the intended behavior for a standard password login system and prevents users from regaining access.
review.option_a: Without an unlock mechanism, any user who makes 5 failed attempts is permanently locked out, requiring manual administrative intervention that is not specified in the requirements.
review.option_b: Add the requirement: "The system SHALL automatically unlock a locked account after a period of 15 minutes has elapsed since the last failed attempt."

review.explanation: The requirement states that the account locks when "the number of failed attempts on an account reaches 5", but it does not specify if this count is cumulative over time, resets after a successful login, or resets after a certain period. A tester cannot determine if a 6th failure after a successful login should trigger a lockout.
review.option_a: Keeping the text as written implies the counter is cumulative and never resets, which may lead to permanent lockouts for users who eventually succeed but make occasional errors later.

review.title: Ambiguous administrator exemption scope
review.explanation: The requirement states that for an administrator, "the system does not lock the account", but it is unclear if this means the lockout mechanism is entirely disabled (allowing infinite retries) or if it only exempts them from the *consequence* of being locked out while still tracking attempts. It also does not clarify if administrators are subject to the same 5-attempt threshold for other security measures.
review.option_a: Keeping the text as written implies administrators can attempt passwords indefinitely without any account state change, which may be a security risk if the intent was only to prevent denial of service.
review.option_b: Rewrite R5 as: "WHEN a user submits an incorrect password for an administrator account THEN the system denies access and does not increment the failed attempt counter for lockout purposes"

review.title: Missing unlock mechanism

This implies a permanent lockout, which contradicts the typical purpose of a temporary security measure and leaves the system in a state with no defined recovery path.
review.option_a: Keeping the document as written implies that once an account is locked, it remains locked permanently unless manually intervened by an out-of-band process not described in the specification.
review.option_b: Add the requirement: "WHEN an administrator manually unlocks a locked account THEN the system resets the failed attempt counter to 0 and allows the account to accept login attempts"

If the property record is retained in the database for audit purposes, it is not removed from the active data set (assuming 'active data set' and 'database' are distinct contexts where removal implies deletion from active but retention implies keeping in DB, but typically 'removed from active' allows 'retained in db'. However, 'removed' usually means gone from the primary store. Let's look closer. 'property_record_removed' means removed from *active data set*. 'property_record_retained_in_db' means remains in *database*. These are not necessarily mutually exclusive in all systems (soft delete), but usually 'removed' implies it's not in the active view. The prompt asks for facts that hold in EVERY snapshot. Is it possible for a record to be removed from active but retained in DB? Yes (soft delete). Is it possible for it to be retained in DB but not removed from active? No, if it's active, it's in the DB. So (not property_record_removed) implies property_record_retained_in_db? Not necessarily, it could be in neither? Unlikely. Let's stick to stronger logical implications based on standard definitions. 

Actually, let's re-evaluate 'property_record_removed' vs 'property_record_retained_in_db'. 
If a record is 'removed', it is generally no longer in the primary accessible store. 
If it is 'retained', it is still there. 
These are often opposites in the context of 'active' vs 'archive'. 
However, without a specific definition linking 'active data set' and 'database', we cannot be 100% certain they are mutually exclusive or that one implies the negation of the other in a formal logical sense without assumptions about the system architecture. 

Let's look at 'deletion_attempted'. 
If deletion is initiated, it was attempted. 
If deletion is denied, it was attempted. 
So: (=> deletion_initiated deletion_attempted) and (=> deletion_denied deletion_attempted). 
Thus: (=> deletion_attempted (or deletion_initiated deletion_denied ...?)) No, attempt is the superset. 
Fact: If deletion is initiated, a deletion was attempted. 
Fact: If deletion is denied, a deletion was attempted. 

Let's refine the list with high-confidence semantic implications:

1. If deletion is initiated, a deletion was attempted.
2. If deletion is confirmed, a deletion was initiated.
3. If deletion is denied, a deletion was attempted.
4. If the property is deleted (process completed), the property record is removed from the active data set.
5. If the property is deleted (process completed), a confirmation message is displayed (usually part of 'completed'). Wait, 'completed' might just mean the state change. 'confirmation_message_displayed' is a UI event. Is it necessary? Often yes, but is it *definitional*? Maybe not. 
6. If deletion is denied, the property is not deleted.
7. If deletion is confirmed, the property is not denied.

Let's stick to the most robust ones:
- (=> deletion_confirmed deletion_initiated)
- (=> deletion_initiated deletion_attempted)
- (=> deletion_denied deletion_attempted)
- (=> property_deleted property_record_removed)
- (=> deletion_denied (not property_deleted))
- (=> deletion_confirmed (not deletion_denied))
- (=> property_deleted (not deletion_denied))

Also:
- If the property is hidden from UI, is it deleted? Not necessarily (could be manually hidden). 
- If the property record is removed, is it hidden from UI? Yes, if it's not in the active data set, the UI (which reads from active data set) cannot show it. So (=> property_record_removed property_hidden_from_ui).

Let's verify (=> property_record_removed property_hidden_from_ui). If the record is gone from the active data set, the UI, which displays data from the active data set, will not display it. This seems semantically sound for 'hidden from user interface' in this context. 

Let's verify (=> property_deleted property_record_removed). 'Deletion process completed' implies the deletion happened. Deletion implies removal. Sound.

Let's verify (=> deletion_confirmed (not deletion_denied)). You can't confirm and be denied for the same logical flow step simultaneously in a single state snapshot of the outcome? Or rather, the *outcome* is either success or denial. If confirmed, the request is accepted, so it is not denied. Sound.

Let's verify (=> deletion_initiated deletion_attempted). Initiation is a form of attempt. Sound.

Let's verify (=> deletion_denied deletion_attempted). Denial is a response to an attempt. Sound.

One more: 
(=> property_deleted confirmation_message_displayed)? 
'Deletion process completed' usually entails feedback. But is it *necessary*? A background job might complete deletion without a UI message. The symbol 'property_deleted' refers to the state of the property, not the UI. 'confirmation_message_displayed' is UI. So this is not a necessary logical truth about the *meaning* of the symbols, but about the system behavior. Exclude.

(=> property_deleted redirected_to_properties_list)? Same issue. UI behavior. Exclude.

(=> property_record_removed property_hidden_from_ui)? 
If the record is removed from the *active data set*, the UI (which queries the active data set) will not show it. This is a structural implication. I will include it.

Final List:
1. (=> deletion_confirmed deletion_initiated)
2. (=> deletion_initiated deletion_attempted)
3. (=> deletion_denied deletion_attempted)
4. (=> property_deleted property_record_removed)
5. (=> deletion_denied (not property_deleted))
6. (=> deletion_confirmed (not deletion_denied))
7. (=> property_record_removed property_hidden_from_ui)

review.option_b: Rewrite D2 as: "WHEN a Property Owner confirms deletion, THE Platform SHALL mark the Property as deleted so that it is no longer visible in the user interface"

If 'removed' means it is gone from the active set, and 'retained' means it remains in storage, these can technically coexist in a soft-delete scenario. However, looking at the standard interpretation of 'removed from active data set' vs 'retained in database', they are often mutually exclusive states of the *record's availability*. But strictly, 'removed from active data set' does not logically preclude 'retained in database' (soft delete). Let's re-evaluate. If 'property_record_removed' means the record is gone from the 'active data set' (e.g., UI/backend API), it can still be in the DB. If 'property_record_retained_in_db' means it is still in the DB, they can coexist. Therefore, no mutual exclusion fact is certain. Let's look for other facts.

Re-evaluating mutual exclusion: Is there a symbol that implies the record is physically deleted? 'property_deleted' implies the process completed. Usually, 'deleted' implies the record is gone. If 'property_deleted' is true, is 'property_record_retained_in_db' false? In many systems, 'delete' means physical or logical deletion. If it's logical, it is retained. If physical, it is not. Without knowing the type of deletion, we cannot assert mutual exclusion between `property_deleted` and `property_record_retained_in_db`. However, `property_record_removed` explicitly says 'removed from... active data set'. `property_record_retained_in_db` says 'remains present in the database storage'. These are distinct locations/layers. A record can be removed from the active set but retained in the DB. So no contradiction.

Let's look at `property_hidden_from_ui` and `property_deleted`. If `property_deleted` is true, the property is gone, so it is hidden. This is already listed.

Let's look at `deletion_denied` and `deletion_confirmed`. If deletion is denied, it wasn't confirmed (or the confirmation was invalid). But `deletion_denied` is a rejection. `deletion_confirmed` is the user action. A user can confirm, and then the system can deny it (e.g. due to permission check after prompt). So they can co-exist in time, but in a snapshot? If the state is 'denied', has it been 'confirmed'? The symbol `deletion_confirmed` usually refers to the user's action. If the system denies, the user likely did confirm. So no negation.

Let's look at `authorization_error_displayed` and `deletion_denied`. If an authorization error is displayed, the deletion was likely denied due to authorization. But `deletion_denied` is a general rejection. Does `authorization_error_displayed` imply `deletion_denied`? Usually, an error display for authorization failure indicates the request was rejected. So yes, likely.

Let's look at `property_deleted` and `deletion_denied`. These are mutually exclusive outcomes of an attempt. If it was denied, it wasn't successfully completed. If it was successfully completed, it wasn't denied.

Let's look at `deletion_initiated` and `deletion_attempted`. Initiating a process is a form of attempting it. So `deletion_initiated` implies `deletion_attempted`.

Let's look at `property_belongs_to_user`. If deletion is denied due to authorization, it might be because the property doesn't belong to the user? No, authorization can be complex. But if `property_deleted` is true, it is a fact that the property belonged to the user (since they initiated and confirmed). So `property_deleted` implies `property_belongs_to_user`.

review.title: Removal vs Retention
review.explanation: D2 states the platform SHALL "remove the Property record from the Platform", while D4 states the platform SHALL "retain Property records in the database". These requirements demand incompatible outcomes for the same action: the record cannot be both removed and retained.
review.option_a: The system physically deletes the data, violating the audit requirement in D4.
review.option_b: Rewrite D2 as: "WHEN a Property Owner confirms deletion, THE Platform SHALL mark the Property as deleted so that it is no longer visible in the user interface"

rewrite.text: WHEN a Property is deleted, THE Platform SHALL ensure the Property is not visible in the user interface but remains accessible for audit purposes

review.title: Implementation detail
review.explanation: The requirement prescribes a specific implementation technique ("implement soft deletion") and internal storage state ("retain... in the database") rather than observable behavior. A tester cannot verify the internal database state or the specific technique used, only the visible effect.
review.option_a: The system must use a specific database flag or table structure, which is not observable by a user.
review.option_b: Rewrite D4 as: "WHEN a Property is deleted, THE Platform SHALL ensure the Property is not visible in the user interface but remains accessible for audit purposes"

If a property record physically exists in the database storage, it has not been successfully processed for deletion.
If a property is successfully processed for deletion, it is not visible in the user interface.
If the deletion is denied, the property record is not removed from the active platform data view.
If the deletion is denied, the property is not successfully processed for deletion.
If the deletion is denied, the success confirmation message is not displayed.
If the deletion is denied, the user is not redirected to the properties list as a success action.
If the deletion is denied, an authorization error message is displayed.
If the deletion is denied, the property record still physically exists in the database storage.
If the deletion is denied, the property remains visible in the user interface.
If the property record is removed from the active platform data view, the deletion has been confirmed.
If the property is successfully processed for deletion, the deletion has been confirmed.
If the deletion is confirmed, the property record is removed from the active platform data view.
If the deletion is confirmed, the property is successfully processed for deletion.
If the deletion is confirmed, the confirmation prompt has been displayed.
If the deletion is confirmed, the deletion was initiated.
If the deletion is confirmed, the property belongs to the owner.
If the deletion is confirmed, the deletion was not denied.

If the deletion is confirmed, the property record does not physically exist in the database storage (assuming logical deletion implies physical removal or the state 'property_deleted' implies the record is gone from active storage context, but strictly 'property_deleted' is 'successfully processed'. Usually logical deletion keeps the record. However, 'property_record_in_database' is 'physically exists'. If 'property_deleted' means the process is complete, and the system uses logical deletion, the record might still be in the DB. Let's look at the definitions. 'property_record_removed' is logical deletion. 'property_deleted' is state successfully processed. If it's logical deletion, the record is still in the database. So (=> property_deleted (not property_record_in_database)) is NOT necessarily true. It depends on the implementation. The prompt says 'logical deletion' for removed. So the record is likely still in the DB. Therefore, we cannot claim the record is NOT in the DB. We can only claim it's not visible. Let's stick to the visibility and state definitions.)
If a property record is removed from the active Platform data view, it is not visible to the user in the user interface.
If a property has been successfully processed for deletion, it is not visible to the user in the user interface.

If a property record is removed from the active Platform data view, it is not physically present in the active view, but this does not necessarily mean it is removed from the database; however, logically, if it is removed from the 'active' view, it is not visible. More strongly, if the record is removed from the active view, it is not in the active set. The symbol `property_record_in_database` implies physical existence. `property_record_removed` implies logical deletion. A logically deleted record is not visible in the UI.
If the deletion is denied, the property record is not removed from the active Platform data view.
If the deletion is denied, the property has not been successfully processed for deletion.

If a property record is physically present in the database, it exists in storage. This is a tautology by definition, but we can link it to visibility only if we assume the UI reflects the DB. However, the prompt asks for facts that hold in EVERY snapshot based on meaning. `property_record_in_database` means it is in the DB. `property_visible_in_ui` means it is in the UI. There is no logical necessity that DB presence implies UI visibility (e.g., caching, filters), nor that UI visibility implies DB presence (e.g., mock data). review.title: Removal vs Retention
review.explanation: D2 states the Platform SHALL "remove the Property record from the Platform", while D4 states the Platform SHALL "retain Property records in the database". These requirements demand incompatible outcomes for the same action: the record cannot be both removed and retained.
review.option_a: The system physically deletes the data, violating the audit requirement in D4, or it retains the data, violating the removal requirement in D2.
review.option_b: Rewrite D2 as: "WHEN a Property Owner confirms deletion, THE Platform SHALL mark the Property as deleted so that it is no longer visible in the user interface"

rewrite.text: WHEN a Property is deleted, THE Platform SHALL ensure the Property data remains available for audit purposes while being hidden from the user interface

review.title: Implementation Prescribed
review.explanation: The requirement prescribes a specific implementation technique ("implement soft deletion") and internal storage state ("retain Property records in the database") rather than observable behavior. A tester cannot verify the internal database state or the specific deletion mechanism, only the visible result.
review.option_a: The system must use a specific database flag or table structure, which may not be testable via the user interface and restricts technical choices.
review.option_b: Rewrite D4 as: "WHEN a Property is deleted, THE Platform SHALL ensure the Property data remains available for audit purposes while being hidden from the user interface"

rewrite.text: WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is unavailable, THE Order System SHALL reject the order and notify the customer that the items are out of stock.

review.title: Backorder placement conflict
review.explanation: R2 requires the system to "place the order on backorder" when inventory is unavailable, while R3 states the system "SHALL NOT place any order on backorder". These requirements directly contradict each other in the specific situation where an order is submitted and inventory is unavailable.
review.option_a: Keeping the requirements as written makes it impossible to define the correct system behavior for orders with unavailable inventory, as the system is simultaneously required to and forbidden from placing orders on backorder.
review.option_b: Rewrite R2 as: "WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is unavailable, THE Order System SHALL reject the order and notify the customer that the items are out of stock."

rewrite.text: WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is unavailable, THE Order System SHALL reject the order and refund any associated payments.

review.title: Missing handling for unavailable inventory
review.explanation: The user story states the customer should "either receive my goods or get my money back". While R1 covers receiving goods, there is no requirement defining what happens to the customer's payment or the order status when inventory is unavailable and the order cannot be fulfilled (assuming backorder is removed per R3).
review.option_a: Without this requirement, the system's behavior for failed orders is undefined, potentially leaving customers without goods or a refund, violating the user story.
review.option_b: Add the requirement: "WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is unavailable, THE Order System SHALL reject the order and refund any associated payments."

review.explanation: R2 requires the system to "place the order on backorder" when inventory is unavailable, while R3 states the system "SHALL NOT place any order on backorder". review.title: Missing cancellation validation
review.explanation: The user story implies that customers can cancel orders to get their money back, but there is no requirement defining when an order can be canceled. A tester cannot determine if the system should allow cancellation after fulfillment has begun or if it should reject such requests.
review.option_a: Without this requirement, the system may allow cancellation of already-fulfilled orders, leading to financial loss and operational errors.
review.option_b: Add the requirement: "WHEN a customer requests to cancel an order AND the order has not yet been fulfilled, THE Order System SHALL cancel the order. review.title: Backorder placement conflict

rewrite.text: WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is unavailable, THE Order System SHALL reject the order and refund any associated payments.

review.title: Missing handling for unavailable inventory

review.option_b: Add the requirement: "WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is unavailable, THE Order System SHALL reject the order and refund any associated payments."

rewrite.text: WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is unavailable, THE Order System SHALL reject the order and notify the customer that the items are out of stock.

review.title: Backorder placement conflict
review.explanation: R2 requires the system to "place the order on backorder" when inventory is unavailable, while R3 states the system "SHALL NOT place any order on backorder". These requirements directly contradict each other in the specific situation where an order is submitted and inventory is unavailable.
review.option_a: Keeping the requirements as written makes it impossible to define the correct system behavior for orders with unavailable inventory, as the system is simultaneously required to and forbidden from placing them on backorder.
review.option_b: Rewrite R2 as: "WHEN an order is submitted AND inventory is unavailable, THE Order System SHALL reject the order and notify the customer that the items are out of stock."

rewrite.text: WHEN a customer requests to cancel an order AND the order has not yet been fulfilled, THE Order System SHALL cancel the order.

review.title: Missing cancellation validation
review.explanation: The user story implies that customers can cancel orders to get their money back, but there is no requirement defining when an order can be canceled. It is unclear if an order can be canceled after it has already been fulfilled, which would conflict with the goal of receiving goods.
review.option_a: Without this requirement, the system might allow customers to cancel and refund orders that have already been shipped and delivered, leading to financial loss and operational confusion.
review.option_b: Add the requirement: "WHEN a customer requests to cancel an order AND the order has not yet been fulfilled, THE Order System SHALL cancel the order."
